content.text: Radio waves, light, X-rays—they seem very different, but they're all part of the same family: electromagnetic waves. The electromagnetic spectrum spans an enormous range of wavelengths and frequencies, from radio waves longer than football fields to gamma rays smaller than atoms. Understanding this spectrum is key to modern technology, medicine, and communication.
are transverse waves consisting of oscillating electric and magnetic fields.
All travel at the speed of light in a vacuum:
Do NOT require a medium (can travel through vacuum)
Transfer energy from source to absorber
The EM spectrum is the full range of electromagnetic waves, arranged by wavelength or frequency.

The Relationship Between Wavelength, Frequency, and Energy

All EM waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum (3 x 10^8 m/s) but differ in wavelength and frequency. Higher frequency means shorter wavelength, higher energy, and greater potential danger.

"Different EM waves are fundamentally different things"
— They're all the same type of wave, just different frequencies/wavelengths.
— They travel best in a vacuum. Light from stars reaches us through empty space.
— They're crucial for mobile phones, WiFi, and satellite communication.
— Radio waves and visible light are not harmful at normal levels. Only higher frequencies (UV, X-rays, gamma) are ionising and dangerous.
— Infrared is invisible to all humans, though some animals can detect it.
EM spectrum (increasing frequency): radio, microwaves, infrared, visible, UV, X-rays, gamma
Higher frequency = shorter wavelength = more energy = more dangerous

Gamma rays have much higher frequency and energy

than radio waves. This makes them ionising — they carry enough energy to remove electrons from atoms, damaging DNA and cells, which can cause cancer and mutations. Radio waves are non-ionising and do not carry enough energy to damage cells. (comparison)
EM waves are oscillating electric and magnetic fields
that do not require a medium; they can travel through the vacuum of space. Sound is a mechanical wave that requires particles to propagate, and space is a vacuum with no particles. (comparison)
